1:15.t: Compunction is divided into many kinds: to wit, when every sin is of penitent men in particular bewailed: whereof the prophet Jeremy, in the person of penitent sinners, speaketh thus: Mine eye hath brought forth divisions of waters. 1:29.t: For the stars of this night are overshadowed with darkness, when even they that already shine with great virtues, still bear something of the dimness of sin, while they struggle against it, so that they even shine with great lustre of life, and yet still draw along with unwillingness some remains of the night. Which as we have said is done with this view, that the mind in advancing to the eminence of its righteousness, may through weakness be the better strengthened, and may in a more genuine manner shine in goodness by the same cause, whereby, to the humbling of it, little defects overcloud it even against its will. 1:34.t: "The waters increased and elevated the ark high above the earth. And the waters drenched the earth, filling it and covering everything." The increased waters of baptism and faith also elevated the church throughout the world from an appetite for earthly things to the hope and desire for heavenly life. Hence, tossing the church about with great tribulations, the more vigorously these waters fill the earth, the higher they push it toward seeking the joys of the other life. This is well illustrated in sacred history when it is said, "The Amorites held the children of Dan to the mountains, nor did they permit them to descend to the plains." Amorite, of course, means "bitter," whereas Dan is translated as "judge" or "judgment." […]

2:7.t: The reader of the present lesson was reading it thus: "and the people feared the Lord all the days of Joshua", but we have: "and the people served the Lord all the days of Joshua, and all the days of their elders, who were of longer days after Joshua". We must therefore understand that each one of us secures it for himself, whether he be in good days or in evil, and whether he have "the days of Joshua" — that is, the days of the righteous — or have the days of the impious. For if we understand "the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world", and offer it our souls to enlighten, or if "the sun of righteousness" rise upon us and "enlighten the world" of our soul, then we too have "the days of Jesus" Christ, the days of salvation. […]

2:8.t: The death of Jesus too has been read to us. That he, indeed, "the son of Nun", "died" is no wonder; for he paid what was owed to nature. But since we had undertaken to refer these things, which were read concerning the son of Nun, to our Lord Jesus Christ, we must see how it may fittingly be said even of him that: "Jesus died". I think — speaking this too, however, according to the authority of Scripture — that in some Jesus lives, but in some he has "died". In Paul Jesus lives, and in Peter, and in all those who can deservedly say: "and now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me". And again he says: "for me to live is Christ, and to die is gain". In such men as these, therefore, Jesus is deservedly said to "live". But in whom has "Jesus died"? […]

2:10.t: "And the children of Israel did what was wicked before God". Almighty God, our ruler, grant that it may never happen to us that Jesus Christ, after he has risen from the dead, should again die in us. For what does it profit me if in others he lives by virtue and in me he dies by the weakness of sin? What does it profit me if in me and in my heart he does not live, and if in me he does not accomplish the works of life? What does it profit me if in another he is nourished and refreshed by good pursuits, by good faith, by good works, but in me and in my heart he is in a manner suffocated and slain by evil thoughts and unspeakable desires, by the worst pursuits? […]

2:11.t: "And it served", it says, "the Baalim, and they forsook the Lord God of their fathers". These things indeed the ancients did, but since the things that are written are said to have been written not for their sake, but "for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come", let us see whether these things may seem to be said in greater part of us than of them. And do you wish to see that not by me, but by the Apostle these things are expounded as being about us? Hear himself what he says: "but in Elijah what does the Scripture say, how he pleads with God against Israel? Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have torn down your altars, and I am left alone, and they seek my life. But what does the divine answer say to him? […]

2:12.t: After the death of Joshua the son of Nave [Nun] they forsook the God of their fathers and served idols, Baalim and Ashtaroth; and the Lord in anger delivered them up to the hands of plunderers, and they continued to be plundered by them and to be sold to their adversaries, and [they] could not at all stand before their enemies. Wherever they went forth, his hand was upon them for evil, and they were greatly distressed. And after this God sets judges, the same as our censors, over them. But not even these did they continue steadfastly to obey. So soon as one of the judges died, they proceeded to transgress more than their fathers had done by going after the gods of others and serving and worshiping them. Therefore the Lord was angry. […]

"And they adored", it says, "strange gods, the gods of the nations who were round about them, and they provoked the Lord to anger". See how much sins accomplish, that we who sin are said to provoke to anger him in whom there is not only no affection of anger, but not even any other passible movement. Truly he remains unchangeable in his nature and is never disturbed by the affections of anger; but I, through the things in which I transgress, decree anger for myself, just as the Apostle says, teaching this very thing: "but according to your hardness and impenitent heart you treasure up", he says, "for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will render to each one according to his works".

2:13.t: Therefore "they provoked the Lord to anger, and forsook the Lord, they worshipped Baal and Astarte. And the Lord was angry with fury against Israel, and delivered them into the hands of plunderers". As long as one serves God, he is not "delivered into the hands of plunderers". But when he has "forsaken the Lord" and has begun to serve his own passions, then it is said of him that: "God delivered them into passions of ignominy", and again: "he delivered them into a reprobate mind, that they should do those things which are not fitting". Why? […]

2:23.t: You may read that it was possible for the nations to be exterminated at once out of the land which was given to the children of Israel, and yet that God willed it to be gradually effected. And one may meet with a thousand other incidents, the past or the future possibility of which we might readily admit, and yet be unable to produce any proofs of their having ever really happened. Accordingly, it would not be right for us to deny the possibility of a man's living without sin, on the ground that amongst men none can be found except Him who is in His nature not man only, but also God, in whom we could prove such perfection of character to have existed.
2:23.s: ON THE SPIRIT AND THE LETTER 1

2:23.t: All these beautiful things are born from a man’s perceiving his own weakness. For from this, because of his longing for help, he turns to God with beseechings. And as he brings near his spirit unto God, He comes nigh unto him with His gifts. And He does not take away from him His inspiration, because of his great humility. For as a widow unto the judge, he cries at all times: avenge me on my adversary. Therefore God, the merciful, necessarily will delay his petitions, that he have the better reason to approach unto Him. And because of his need he will constantly remain at the fountain of help, while God grants some of his demands quickly, others not: [He grants] those concerning which He knows that they are necessary for life, the rest He delays. […]

3:1.t: But the blessed David recognizes that sometimes this departure of which we have spoken, and (as it were) desertion by God may be to some extent to our advantage, so that he was unwilling to pray, not that he might not be absolutely forsaken by God in anything (for he was aware that this would have been disadvantageous both to himself and to human nature in its course towards perfection) but he rather entreated that it might be in measure and degree, saying "Forsake me not utterly" as if to say in other words: I know that thou dost forsake thy saints to their advantage, in order to prove them, for in no other way could they be tempted by the devil, unless they were for a little forsaken by Thee. […]

In all these phrases then there is proof that Divine grace ever stirs up the will of man, not so as to protect and defend it in all things in such a way as to cause it not to fight by its own efforts against its spiritual adversaries, the victor over whom may set it down to God's grace, and the vanquished to his own weakness, and thus learn that his hope is always not in his own courage but in the Divine assistance, and that he must ever fly to his Protector. And to prove this not by our own conjecture but by still clearer passages of Holy Scripture let us consider what we read in Joshuah the son of Nun: "The Lord," it says, "left these nations and would not destroy them, that by them He might try Israel, whether they would keep the commandments of the Lord their God, and that they […]
3:1.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapter 14

3:1.t: God's providence, Peter, in bestowing of his gifts, is wonderful: for often it falleth out, that upon whom he vouchsafeth the greater, he giveth not the less: to the end that always they may have somewhat to mis-like in themselves: so that desiring to arrive unto perfection and yet can not: and labouring about that which they have not obtained, and can not prevail: by this means they become not proud of those gifts which they have received, but do thereby learn that they have not those greater graces of themselves, who of themselves cannot overcome small faults. […]

3:7.t: When "the children of Israel did evil in the sight of God, and forgot the Lord their God," and, forsaking him, "served the Baalim and the groves" of the nations, then, "storing up wrath for themselves," they "were handed over," by the just judgment of God, "into the hands of their enemies," according to what the present reading has declared: "into the hands," it says, "of Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia." Now Cushan-rishathaim is interpreted as "their humiliation". They "were handed over," therefore, "into the hands" of him who would humiliate them. And because they themselves were acting impiously against the Most High upon the high places of the mountains, for that reason they are handed over by him into humiliation. […]

Now therefore let us see what these do who are handed over on account of sin and set in tribulation. Precisely that which is written: "and they cried out to the Lord when they were in tribulation, and he delivered them out of their distresses." "And he led them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and burst their bonds asunder." But each one of us also — even if he be small, even if he be the least, even if he enjoy no dignity in the world — can be afflicted with the vice of pride; and nothing is so foul nor so execrable, as Scripture says, as "a poor man who is proud and a rich man who is a liar." Sometimes, however, this disease of pride penetrates not only the poor of the common people, but strikes even the priestly and Levitical order itself. […]

3:9.t: Now he calls Othniel the Savior, who is interpreted as "the time of God for me". Through this Othniel, therefore, that former people was snatched from the servitude of humiliation, and peace was restored to the people — the peace which pride and the various crimes of the people had for a while put to flight. But since we have said that a certain Cushan-rishathaim can be understood spiritually, both as a king and as one of the adversaries and a prince among the "airy powers," so it seems to me consequent that this Othniel too, who was raised up to deliver the people, is some one of the "heavenly host" and of the archangelic troops which "are sent as a help to those who obtain the inheritance of salvation"; […]

3:10.t: What, then, does Scripture say concerning this Othniel? After it had said that "the children of Israel cried out to the Lord," "the Spirit of the Lord came," it says, "upon Othniel, and he judged Israel." Do you suppose there is among us anyone who so "sends forth to the Lord a cry" so strong and so just that he is worthy to be heard, and the people deserve to receive a judge — and such a judge, one whom the "Spirit of God" may fill, that he may be able to hold to right judgment? Whence also the book itself is called the book of Judges, and in it are described the judges who judged the people. […]

3:11.t: And after this it says: "the land had rest under him as judge for forty years." You see how bountiful is the divine clemency. "For eight years the children of Israel had served" for the offenses of many; "for forty years" they endure in peace for the righteousness of one.

3:12.t: But what is said after this? "And Othniel," it says, "the son of Kenaz, died." I see a perilous matter. "Othniel died." Why? Because the people was now unworthy to have such a judge. Then in what follows, after he had died, it says: "and the children of Israel added," it says, "to do evil in the sight of the Lord; and the Lord strengthened Eglon king of Moab against Israel." Consider that, because they were now unworthy to have such a leader, for that reason the good judge is taken away from them. And because they "did evil in the sight of the Lord," there is stirred up against them a most wicked enemy, "Eglon king of Moab." […]

3:14.t: "And the children of Israel served," it says, "Eglon king of Moab for eighteen years." Observe that divine Scripture indicates even the measures of the punishment; there it says "for eight years" and here "for eighteen." Now it is certain that according to the measure of the sin and the delay of our conversion the times of chastisement too are determined.

3:15.t: For these "eighteen years" of servitude also passed, and it is not recounted that "they cried out to the Lord" or were converted from their wickedness, but after eighteen years it is again said that: "the children of Israel cried out to the Lord, and the Lord raised up for them a Savior, Ehud the son of Gera, the son of Gemini, a man ambidextrous." Behold what manner of man this is who is raised up to save Israel! He has nothing left-handed in himself, but has both hands as a right hand; for this is what is meant by "ambidextrous." […]

To the rule of Ehud the ambidextrous is joined the rule of Shamgar. But let us see how Ehud, who is interpreted "praise," brought his rule to a close. The narrative has taught us those things which are written concerning Eglon the king, how this most wise Ehud, using a certain artifice and, so to speak, a cunning but praiseworthy deception, slew Eglon the tyrant, who is interpreted "whirling" or "of the wheel-track." Such, then, ought the judges of our people also to be, as was that Ehud who is interpreted "praise," so that they may cut down all the whirling motions and wheel-tracks of the evil path and destroy the king of the Midianites. Now the Midianites are interpreted "flowing" or "outpouring." […]

Therefore I say plainly that the just man has two right hands. Indeed even that Ehud, who is written of in the book of Judges, is said to have two right hands for this reason, because he was just, and he killed that very fat king.

Do you wish to know that the just man has no left hand? When Moses, in the type of the cross, lifted both his hands to heaven, it is not written, "Aaron was at his right and Hur at his left," but that on this side stood Aaron and on that side Hur. In the book of Judges too, that leader Ehud, whose mystery is manifold and great, who had a sword upon his thigh, and had cut off desires, and had also run through with his blade his very fat and gross adversary, is for that reason written "amphoterodexios," that is, having both hands as a right hand, whom in Latin we may call "ambidextrous."

Those are they then who are figurately spoken of in holy Scripture as a0mfoterode/cion, i.e., ambidextrous, as Ehud is described in the book of Judges "who used either hand as the right hand." And this power we also can spiritually acquire, if by making a right and proper use of those things which are fortunate, and which seem to be "on the right hand," as well as of those which are unfortunate and as we call it "on the left hand," we make them both belong to the right side, so that whatever turns up proves in our case, to use the words of the Apostle, "the armour of righteousness." […]

3:16.t: But let us see what this "ambidextrous" judge does. "The children of Israel sent," it says, "gifts to Eglon king of the Moabites by the hand of Ehud"; "and Ehud made himself a sword sharpened on both sides, of the length of an extended palm, and girded it to himself upon his right thigh." You see that everything is right-handed which this "ambidextrous" "Ehud" carries out: he is right-handed both in hands and right-handed in feet. For he carries the sword on his right thigh, that he may come to the "king of Moab" and slay him. […]

3:30.t: Now, judges were established over them from the time they took over the promised land and before the monarchy began. And even during this era, the children of iniquity, that is, foreign foes, afflicted them, for we read they had now peace, now war. Even so, you can find periods of peace in the age of the judges longer than that of Solomon, who reigned forty years. Specifically, under the judge named Ehud, there were eighty years of peace.

3:31.t: But having briefly gone back over these matters from the earlier reading — that is, over the end of Ehud — let us now see what sort the beginning of Shamgar is also, who is there interpreted "stranger." For it is true that all who are men of God are strangers in this world and sojourners upon the earth, just as was also he who said that: "I am a sojourner with thee upon the earth and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were". And so the Holy Spirit there calls this Shamgar too a sojourner — that is, here. For what is "there" to the Holy Spirit, who is in the heavens, is "here" to us. What, then, is said of Shamgar? "He smote", it says, "the Philistines, six hundred men, with the handle — or "foot" — of a plow". I see another kind of praise in Shamgar: this one fights with a "plow". […]

4:1.t: But what is added after this? "And the children of Israel", it says, "added to do evil in the sight of the Lord; and Ehud was dead". Undoubtedly in these matters too there is preserved that observation which we pointed out in the preceding passages: that for the sins of the people the good leader of the people dies. For when they have been made unworthy and have "done evil in the sight of God", the man of God will be taken away from them. But perhaps our people will say: when is the Church of God without a judge? Even if the former departs, another is supplied. Perhaps we shall say something bold, yet we say what is written. Not always is the prince of the people and judge of the Church given by the judgment of God, but according as our merits demand. […]

4:2.t: "And the prince", it says, "of the army of Jabin was Sisera, and he himself dwelt in Harosheth of the Gentiles, and he had nine hundred iron chariots. And the children of Israel cried out to the Lord". In this too there is likewise kept that observation which we designated above: that the children of Israel do not know how "to cry out to the Lord", except when "they have been delivered into the hands of Jabin", or when they are afflicted through his "prince of the army, Sisera", who "had", it says, "nine hundred iron chariots", by which of course the people of stiff neck was afflicted. Now "Sisera" is interpreted "vision of a horse." For he is the "animal" and not the "spiritual" man, who sees nothing except those things which are "animal"; […]
Sisara [Sisera]: exclusion of joy, or taking away one who withdraws, or vision of a horse.
4:2.s: On Hebrew Names, The Song of Deborah

4:4.t: Let us see, then, whether perhaps through these things we may be taught something worthy, as also from the other Scriptures, concerning the more hidden mysteries. First, this very fact that, although many men are reported to have been judges in Israel, of none of them is it said that he was a "prophet" except of "Deborah the woman." Even the very first surface of the letter itself furnishes no small consolation to the female sex in this, and it summons them, that they should by no means despair, on account of the weakness of their sex, of being able to become capable even of the grace of prophecy, but that they should understand and believe that purity of mind, not diversity of sex, merits this grace. But let us see what secret of the inner understanding also breathes forth here. […]

We pass from questions to questions and from mysteries to mysteries, and while we can scarcely and with difficulty explain each of the first things, more difficult matters follow upon the difficult ones — matters which do not so much require the eloquence of human talent as they demand the inspiration of divine grace. For without doubt the hearer will ask — since indeed there is that saying of the Apostle Paul which declares: "all Scripture divinely inspired is useful for teaching, for reproof, for instruction which is in righteousness" — what this Scripture has in itself (which we likewise without doubt confess to be divinely inspired) that may yield to us "for instruction," that may yield "for reproof," that may yield "for discipline," that may yield "for righteousness." […]

And in order that it may not seem as if only one widow had fulfilled this inimitable work, it seems in no way doubtful that there were many others of equal or almost equal virtue, for good seed corn usually bears many ears filled with grains. Do not doubt, then, that that ancient seedtime was fruitful in the characters of many women. But as it would be tedious to include all, consider some, and especially Deborah, whose virtue Scripture records for us.For she showed not only that widows have no need of the help of a man, inasmuch as she, not at all restrained by the weakness of her sex, undertook to perform the duties of a man, and did even more than she had undertaken. […]

For nothing, nothing is more powerful than a pious and sensible woman to bring a man into proper order, and to mould his soul as she will. For he will not endure friends, or teachers, or rulers, as he will his partner advising and counseling him, since the advice carries even some pleasure with it, because she who gives the counsel is greatly loved. I could tell of many hard and disobedient men who have been softened in this way. For she who shares his table, his bed, and his embraces, his words and secrets, his comings in and goings out, and many other things, who is entirely given up and joined to him, as it is likely that a body would be joined to a head, if she happen to be discreet and well attuned, will go beyond and excel all others in the management of her husband. […]
4:4.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 61

4:5.t: But let us also consider this — where the prophecy is said to "reside" and where its place is described. "Under a palm tree," it says, "between the middle of Ramah and the middle of Bethel." Prophecy has its seat "under a palm tree," because "the righteous man," says David, "will flourish like a palm tree" — through this, that prophecy leads the one instructed by its teachings to the "palm of the heavenly calling of God, in Christ Jesus our Lord." And it is said to sit "between the middle of Ramah and the middle of Bethel." "Ramah" is interpreted as "heights". "Bethel," however, as "the house of God". See in what places "prophecy" is said to "reside" — between the heights and the house of God. […]

4:6.t: This prophecy, therefore, first of all, it says, "sent and called Barak to herself." Now "Barak" is interpreted as "flashing". But a flashing is that which has light indeed, but not lasting; for it shines forth for a little while and ceases. This Barak, therefore, seems to me to bear the figure of the former people, who first of all was called through prophecy and invited to hear the utterances of God and to receive the gifts of the divine law — who indeed shone and flashed in the splendor of the law for a brief time, but did not long endure nor was able to obtain the continuous brightness of the light. […]

And in time of peace there is no complaint, and no fault is found in this woman, whereas most of the judges were causes of no small sins to the people. But when the Canaanites, a people fierce in battle and rich in troops, successively joined them, showed a horrible disposition against the people of the Jews, this widow, before all others, made all the preparations for war. And to show that the needs of the household were not dependent on the public resources but rather that public duties were guided by the discipline of home life, she brings forth from her home her son as a leader of the army, that we may acknowledge that a widow can train a warrior; […]

4:8.t: And lastly, her son Barak shows the chief part of the victory was in the hands of a woman when he said, "If you will not go with me I will not go, because I do not know on what day the Lord will send his angel with me." How great, then, was the might of that woman to whom the leader of the army says, "If you will not go I will not go." How great, I say, the fortitude of the widow who does not protect her son from dangers through motherly affection but rather with the zeal of a mother exhorts her son to go forth to victory, while saying that the decisive point of that victory is in the hand of a woman!

4:17.t: Now it is described that, when according to the admonition of Deborah — that is, of prophecy — Barak pursued Sisera the leader of the Philistines, he himself indeed could not seize him, but there met him "as he fled" a foreign woman, Jael, which woman had previously held a covenant of friendship with him; "to whom," when he had "turned aside" for the sake of hiding, he asked for water to drink, but by her "he was given milk to drink"; and when she had placed him "in hiding" and had covered him with skins, after this she drove a stake, driven in "with a mallet," through his cheeks — or "jaws" — and fixed it fast: and then, "meeting" Barak as he pursued, she "showed Sisera" "now dead" and laid low.

What, then, does all this text of the history show us of the mystery? "Jael," that foreign "woman" concerning whom prophecy said that the victory would come to pass "into the hand of a woman," holds the figure of the Church, which has been gathered from the foreign nations. Now "Jael" is interpreted as "ascent", because in truth there is no other ascent by which one may ascend to heaven except "through the Church of the manifold wisdom of God." She, therefore, is the one who, while she ascends from bodily things to spiritual and from earthly to heavenly, slays Sisera — of whom we have already said above that he holds the figure of the carnal vices and of the "animal" or "earthy" man, because Sisera is interpreted as "the sight of a horse", concerning which Scripture says: "do not […]

4:19.t: But if from this too something seems worthy of being asked by diligent hearers — namely that he is said to have "given him milk to drink" when he had asked for "water" — let us see whether perhaps, according to the mystical or allegorical laws, something of this kind can also be shown concerning this. The food of "milk" is said in the holy Scriptures to be this first moral instruction, which is delivered to beginners as though to "little ones." For at the beginnings the deep and more hidden mysteries are not at once to be delivered to disciples, but the correction of morals, the amendment of discipline, the first elements of religious conduct and of simple faith are delivered to them. […]

4:21.t: So, then, Deborah foretold the event of the battle. Barak, as he was bidden, led forth the army; Jael carried off the triumph, for the prophecy of Deborah fought for her, who in a mystery revealed to us the rising of the church from among the Gentiles, for whom should be found a triumph over Sisera, that is, over the powers opposed to her. For us, then, the oracles of the prophets fought, for us those judgments and arms of the prophets won the victory. And for this reason it was not the people of the Jews but Jael who gained the victory over the enemy. Unhappy, then, was that people which could not follow up by the virtue of faith the enemy, whom it had put to flight. And so by their fault salvation came to the Gentiles; […]

5:1.t: The fourth song is in the book of Judges, concerning which it is written: "And Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam sang on that day, saying: When the leaders in Israel began, in the purpose of the people, bless ye the Lord. Hear, O kings, and give ear," and the rest. But she who sings these things ought to be a bee, whose work is such that both kings and ordinary folk use it for health. For Deborah, who sings this song, is interpreted "a bee," and Barak too along with her: and Barak is interpreted "lightning-flash." And this song is sung after victory, because no one can sing what is perfect until he has conquered his adversaries. So, finally, in the song itself it is said: "Arise, arise, Deborah, rouse up the thousands of the people. Arise, arise, sing a song, arise, Barak." […]
5:1.s: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, PROLOGUE

5:1.t: (Judges 5:1) And Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang. Barak is said to have been a man of Deborah the prophetess. Barak himself is also called Barak son of Lapidoth. For Lapidoth means lightning, and Barak, thunder. Lightning, therefore, because before he avenged Israel against the Canaanites, there was a lightning shining among the people, by merit and prerogative of his deeds: but after he avenged Israel against the Canaanites, he was called Thunder, that is, striking.
5:1.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:2.t: Sisera, together with his army and his "iron chariots", with which he was assailing the people of God, was overcome, as prophecy had foretold would come to pass through Deborah. And after the victory was accomplished "by the hand of a woman", Deborah is recorded to have sung this song as, so to speak, the very praise of that victory. But if we remember the things that were said in the earlier passages — namely, according to the mystical pattern, what figure Deborah is, and Barak likewise, what image the woman Jael holds, who alone cast down the adversary of God's people, what image Sisera himself is, who was laid low by a foreign woman through the power of wood — we understand that all these are sacraments which are brought to completion in the last times and at the end of the age […]

"In the beginning, when the princes were in Israel, in the free wills of the people, bless the Lord". The blessing, he says, with which "we bless the Lord", let it be "in the outset of the princes in Israel", and then afterwards also "in the free wills of the people". For example, when we first begin to come to the worship of God, when we receive the beginning of the word of God and of heavenly teaching, these beginnings must be taken up by us from the "princes of Israel". And by "princes of Israel", that is, of the Christian people, I think we must understand the "angels", whom the Lord says are present to each "least one" in the Church, who are also said "always to see the face of the Father who is in heaven". […]

5:3.t: After this it says: "hear, O kings, and give ear, O satraps: to the Lord I will sing, I will sing praise to the God of Israel". "Hear", it says, "O kings". It calls "kings" those who are summoned to hear the word of God. Exult, O people of God, hearing the insignia of your nobility. You are called to hear the word of God, and you are called not as the common crowd, but as a king. For to you it has been said: "a royal priestly race, a people for acquisition". Therefore, because you are "kings", deservedly is our king Christ the Lord called "king of kings and lord of those who rule". But just as you have exulted over the title of your nobility, so ought you to learn what each of you must do to become a king. Which I will define for you thus, briefly. […]

5:4.t: (Judges 5:4-5) Lord, when you went out from Seir and passed through the regions of Edom, the earth trembled, the heavens and clouds poured down with water. It is said that the Lord went out from Seir and passed through Edom because the Edomites refused to receive his law, so he gave the law of Israel on Mount Sinai. The earth trembled, the heavens and clouds poured down with water. The earthquake of Mount Sinai is described. And when it says, 'The heavens and clouds poured down with water,' it means that in the presence of the Lord, the heavens, as if in fear, emitted sweat, which is said to have dripped down like water. Similarly, the mountains flowed from the presence of the Lord. […]
5:4.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:6.t: (Judges 5:6) In the days of Sangar, the son of Anath, in the days of Jahel, the paths remained empty, and those who entered through them walked along crooked roads. The paths are said to have remained empty because during the time of Sangar, the leader of Israel, the paths had been taken over by enemies of Israel, and they did not dare to freely ascend to the house of the Lord to pray; instead, those who entered through them secretly ascended through crooked streets, out of fear of the enemies. Concerning which enemies Sangar is said to have not fully freed them (Judg. 3:31). […]
5:6.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:7.t: (Judges 5:7) However, the strong ones in Israel ceased, they paused until Deborah, a mother in Israel, arose. These strong ones are the learned teachers and preachers of the law, who are said to have paused, that is, to not have been present, until she arose to teach Israel through preaching, exhortation, and counsel, and to deliver them from their enemies. Deborah also provokes these strong ones in the previous verses to bless the Lord together with her, saying: 'You who willingly offered your lives for the peril of Israel, bless the Lord!' (Verse 2). […]
5:7.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:8.t: (Judges 5:8) The Lord has chosen new wars, and he himself overturns the gates of the enemy. If a shield and a spear appeared among forty thousand Israelites, it is to be understood that he said this as if by swearing an oath, that among forty thousand Israelites neither a shield nor a spear could be found. Therefore, the Lord is said to have chosen new wars, and to have overturned the gates of the enemy because he has made the weak strong and victorious. But it is explained in the previous verse that the Israelites had been despoiled of their weapons by Jabin, king of Canaan, where it is said: And the children of Israel cried to the Lord. He had nine hundred chariots armed with scythes, and for twenty years he severely oppressed them (Judg. IV, 5). […]
5:8.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:9.t: But since we do not undertake to expound the continuation of the song point by point, let us at least, skipping over the sequence of the reading, see what it means where it says: "my heart is toward the things that have been appointed for this Israel". This seems to me to be what it means: my heart and my soul and my sense and my whole mind is bent toward that and looks forward to that "which has been appointed" and which has been prepared "for Israel"; I look forward with my whole mind to that which is to come. For if I bend my mind toward that, all the things that are in this world "I will count as dung, that I may gain Christ", who "has prepared" all those things "which eye has not seen and ear has not heard nor has ascended into the heart of man, for those who love him". […]

(Judges 5:9-10) My heart loves the leaders of Israel. It should be noted that in Hebrew, not leaders, but teachers is read. This is spoken by Deborah in the person of God, that God loves the teachers who study the law of God. Of whom it follows: You who offered yourselves willingly among the people, bless the Lord. Of whom it has also been said above in that place where it says: You who willingly offered your lives from Israel, etc. You who ride on bright donkeys. In Hebrew, female donkeys. And you sit in judgment. In Hebrew, sitting on judgment. And you walk on the road, speak where the chariots collide, and the army of the enemies is suffocated, there the righteousness of the Lord, the strength of Israel, is proclaimed. […]
5:9.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:10.t: "O mighty ones of the people, bless the Lord, you who have mounted upon beasts of burden". What is it "to have mounted upon a beast of burden"? This body of mine is a "beast of burden"; for it was given for the aid of the soul and for its ministry; but it is I, that is, the inner man, "who have mounted upon" this "beast of burden", to whom it is said that I should "bless the Lord". If therefore you have truly mounted upon the body and have been made superior to bodily desires, and the motions of your body are governed by the bridle of the mind and by the direction of the inner man, it is said of you that you "have mounted upon a beast of burden", that you may "bless the Lord". But what is it that follows? "You who sit upon vehicles", it says, "and shine upon she-asses". […]

5:11.t: "There they shall render acts of righteousness to the Lord". That sacrifice is acceptable to the Lord which is offered to God in righteousness and equity, and therefore it is said: "the just have been strengthened in Israel". Among the other nations, indeed, those who are stronger in bodily might are called "mighty" in battle; but in Israel, those who are more just are themselves called the more powerful in wars, because righteousness, even if it be weak in strength, conquers, whereas unrighteousness, even if it have many and strong defenders, is overcome. So therefore in this nation of ours, that is, in the people of God, either through righteousness we overcome or through unrighteousness we are conquered.

(Judges 5:11) Then the people of the Lord went down to the gates and obtained the leadership. The people of the Lord went down to the gates, that is, to the gates of the house of the Lord, because with the Lord blessed and praised at the place of victory, they descended into the house of the Lord to praise the Lord there, offering prayers and sacrifices to Him. But as for the tribe of Issachar, that they were the teachers of the other tribes is shown in the Book of Chronicles, where it says: Of the sons of Issachar, there were men who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do, two hundred chiefs; and all their brethren followed their command (1 Chronicles 12:32). […]
5:11.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:12.t: "Arise, Deborah, arise and rouse up the ten thousands of the people". When does prophecy "arise"? Assuredly at the coming of Christ, and not only does it itself "arise", but it also "rouses up" the peoples to believe. "Lead captivity captive, O son of Abinoam". "Abinoam" is interpreted as "the answer of the father". His son is Barak. He "will take captivity" from the enemies, who has kept the answers of the heavenly Father.

(Judges 5:12) Rise, rise Deborah; rise, speak the Song. It is noteworthy that in Hebrew it is read 'exspergisce,' that is, 'exspergisce' in the spirit of prophecy. Therefore, by the voices of the aforementioned teachers, Deborah is urged to be 'exspergisce' in the spirit of prophecy and praise, and not to cease from praising God. Hence, it follows: Speak the Song. Rise, Barak, and take your captives, son of Abinoam. In Hebrew, it is said: 'Praedare praedam, tuam fili Abinoem.' This statement also warns the same wise men of Barak to plunder the remnants of their enemies, and to bring them to utter destruction, and to commendably acquire the name of victory for themselves.
5:12.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:13.t: "O Lord, humble for me those stronger than I". This is the voice of the faithful, who confess simply that their enemies are stronger, against whom is our struggle and battle, because "our battle is not against flesh and blood" — otherwise our adversary would not be stronger — but since "our wrestling is against principalities and powers and against the rulers of the darkness of this world and against the spiritual forces of wickedness", therefore the prophet says: "O Lord, humble for me those stronger than I". For how should this so great force of spirits not be far more powerful than human frailty? But in this God "helps our weakness", in that the Apostle says: "I can do all things in him who strengthens me, Christ". These powers, then, are indeed stronger than we; […]

(Judges 5:13) Then the remnants of the people were saved. This sentence is to be connected to the previous sentence, which says: Where the righteousness of the Lord is told, the strength of Israel's mercy; because then the remnants of the people were saved. The Lord fought in the strongholds. In Hebrew it is written: The Lord fought for me in the strongholds. And this is the voice of all the people of Israel; for He fought for them against the Egyptians and against the other enemies of Israel. Unde et sequitur.
5:13.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:14.t: (Judges 5:14a) From Ephraim, he destroyed them in Amalek, that is, Joshua, who was from the tribe of Ephraim, destroyed the strong ones, that is, the enemies of Israel, in Amalek, as it is read in the book of Exodus: 'And Joshua defeated Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword, etc.' (Exodus 17:13). And that the same Joshua was from the tribe of Ephraim is shown in the book of Numbers, where it is said: 'From the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Nun' (Numbers 13:9), whom Joshua also calls in the following passages, saying: 'Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun, Joshua.' And after him, that is, Joshua, rising from the tribe of Benjamin, Saul destroyed the people of Amalek, as commanded by the Lord, which Deborah prophesied about Saul in the spirit of prophecy. […]
5:14.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:15.t: (Judges 5:15) The leaders of Issachar were with Deborah. In Hebrew: the princes, that is, the teachers of the Law, were with Deborah to praise the Lord, and Barak followed in the footsteps of the age. It is to be understood that a certain part of them remained with Deborah to praise the Lord, and a part followed Barak to exhort and vanquish Sisera. Who, as if into a precipice, gave himself to danger. Barak, indeed, believing the words of the Lord, gave himself to danger, throwing himself into the torrent Kishon, pursuing and vanquishing the army of Sisera. For in this place a raging torrent is understood as the abyss. Ruben, on the other hand, is divided within himself, and a dispute of noble men is found. It is written in the Book of Judges against itself. […]
5:15.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:16.t: (Judges 5:16) Why do you dwell between two boundaries, to hear the hissing of flocks? It is not read in Hebrew, 'between two', but rather 'between your boundaries', namely the boundaries of your neighboring tribes, to hear the hissing of flocks; as if to say: You desire to preserve the flocks with which you abound, and fear losing them, and you take greater pleasure in hearing their hissing than in striving with your brothers to conquer the enemies of Israel. And because you do this, you proudly resist the command of the Lord. And so it follows the same thing as above: after the division of Reuben, a dispute of the magnanimous is found: because he did evil, despising the authority of the Lord and being proud.
5:16.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:17.t: (Judges 5:17) Gad remained beyond the Jordan. And this is set forth as a reproach because while Reuben remained, Gad remained with him of equal mind. And Dan was free with ships. For seeing that the tribes of Reuben and Gad did not go with their brothers to battle, being terrified by fear, he took flight by being free with ships. Asher dwelt on the seashore and stayed in the ports. Likewise, this is set forth as a reproach because Asher, while dwelling on the seashore, stayed in the ports, choosing instead to flee rather than fight with his brothers.
5:17.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:18.t: (Judges 5:18) Zebulun and Naphtali offered their lives unto death in the region of Morome. In Hebrew, it is 'super regionem Morome'. The meaning is that while the other tribes were unwilling to go, these two tribes offered their lives unto death. In the region of Morome. For Morome is interpreted as 'exalted': they are said to have offered their lives for the sake of the exalted region, that is, for God, and therefore they are praised, while the other tribes are criticized.
5:18.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:19.t: (Judges 5:19) Kings came and fought. The kings of the land of Canaan said, who were subject to King Jabin. The kings of Canaan fought. It repeats the same thing in Tanach. Tanach is indeed a province where the Kishon River is. Near the waters of Megiddo. Megiddo is a city situated on the Kishon River. And what is said, Near the waters of Megiddo, is understood near the Kishon River, the city of Megiddo. Yet they took nothing as plunderers. This is said in mocking, implying that not only did they not obtain any spoils, but they were also unable to save their own lives.
5:19.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:20.t: (Judges 5:20) There was a battle fought against them from heaven. Because in the forty thousand men of Israel a shield and spear could not be found, therefore the Lord fought for them from heaven with hailstones and fire against their enemies. Just as it is also written in the book of Joshua: The stars remained in their order and fought against Sisera (Joshua 10:11). The stars are understood to be the angels who fought against Sisera from heaven.
5:20.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:21.t: (Judges 5:21) The River Kishon swept away their corpses. For there is the place of their downfall; and it is as if one were to ask, where? and the answer is: In the River Kishon, that is, in the Red Sea. Hence it follows: The river Kishon, the river of Kishon. It calls the River Kishon the Red Sea. For Kishon means of old, because ancient miracles were performed there, when the children of Israel passed over and the Egyptians perished. And because the Red Sea vomited forth the dead Egyptians, so that the Israelites saw their dead bodies on the shore of the sea, and the same bodies were carried away by the fish and sea creatures: therefore the River Kishon swept away their corpses, so that the fish and sea creatures of the Red Sea might eat the bodies of the Canaanites, in place of […]
5:21.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:22.t: (Judges 5:22) Then the hooves of the horses fell off, with a powerful force to those fleeing, and headlong to the bravest of the enemies who were rushing. 'Their hooves,' it is read in Hebrew; for it is reported that the hooves of their horses fell off from hailstones from the heavens, that is, from their angels. So the meaning is: If the hooves of the horses fell off from touching the stones, what do you think happened to the riders?
5:22.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:23.t: (Judges 5:23) Cursed be the land of Meroz, said the Angel of the Lord. In Hebrew it is written: Curse Meroz, said the Angel of the Lord. The Angel of the Lord is understood by the Hebrews to be Michael, who commands Deborah to have the people of Israel curse Meroz, that is, the power of the Angel that presided over the Canaanites. For Meroz is interpreted as secret. Therefore, he is commanded to be cursed, that is, anathematized, because while the other angels fought for Israel, he not only did not fight, but also persevered in their adversity. Curse the inhabitants of Meroz, says the Lord's angel. Curse them bitterly because they did not come to help the Lord. They did not come to help the strong Lord.
5:23.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

5:24.t: (Judges 5:24) Blessed among women, Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite. Among women, namely Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Leah, and almost all women. Let her be blessed in the temple, the Lord is understood, so that her memorial may be there, just like Judith. And the reason why she is blessed is given, namely because she acted wisely and prudently, in that she gave milk to the one asking for water. Therefore, she gave milk, so that the fleeing enemy would find a stronger faith in her. And if it is asked why he did not give wine, it must be answered that the house of Rechab do not drink wine, as you have in the prophet Jeremiah (Jer. XXXV, 14).
5:24.s: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

6:1.t: "The land rests" as long as sin rests. But the land is said to be moved—that is, those who dwell in the land—when sins have begun to move and disturb the souls of men. And this is why what the present reading now contains has been written. "And the land rested," it says, "for forty years. And the children of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hands of Midian for seven years. And Midian prevailed over Israel." So then, as long as there was righteousness in the land—that is, in those who dwelt in the land—"the land" is said "to have rested"; but when iniquity increased and "they did evil in the sight of the Lord," then, it says, "the Lord delivered them into the hands of Midian for seven years." […]

6:2.t: But let us see what befalls those who are handed over for their sins. "And the children of Israel made for themselves," it says, "because of the face of Midian, dens in the mountains and in the caves and in the strongholds; and it came to pass, when a man of Israel had sown, that Midian and Amalek and the sons of the East came up against them; and they came upon them and destroyed all the fruits of the land, until one came to Gaza." These things, indeed, that one suffered who was Israel according to the flesh; he sowed the land, but because he had been handed over for his sins to the enemies rising up against him, instead of crops "he reaped corruption." But as for us, who are named Israel according to the spirit, let us consider what such thing can befall us. […]

6:3.t: Granted, the Midianites have gathered against Israel, they who are interpreted as "outside judgment." Granted, these have gathered against Israel, who are outside the judgment of God and "who have sinned outside the law and will perish outside the law." Granted, Amalek too has gathered, who himself is likewise interpreted as "a people that licks up." Granted, this nation too, earthly and given over to the belly and the gullet, has come to make war — a carnal Israel against the spiritual Israel. But what is this, that even the "sons of the East" are mingled with them and are said to come with them to make war on Israel? For my hearer says to me: if it had been written that the "sons" of the West "gathered with them," I would ask nothing; […]

6:11.t: When Jerubbaal, as we read, was beating out wheat under an oak, he received a message from God in order that he might bring the people of God from the power of strangers into liberty. Nor is it a matter of wonder if he was chosen for grace, seeing that even then, being appointed under the shadow of the holy cross and of the adorable Wisdom in the predestined mystery of the future incarnation, he was bringing forth the visible grains of the fruitful corn from their hiding places and was [mystically] separating the elect of the saints from the refuse of the empty chaff. For these elect, as though trained with the rod of truth, laying aside the superfluities of the old man together with his deeds, are gathered in the church as in a winepress. […]

6:19.t: And Gideon, moved by that message, when he heard that, though thousands of the people failed, God would deliver His own from their enemies by means of one man, offered a kid, and according to the word of the Angel, laid its flesh and the unleavened cakes upon the rock, and poured the broth upon them. And as soon as the Angel touched them with the end of the staff which he bore, fire burst forth out of the rock, and so the sacrifice which he was offering was consumed. By which it seems clear that that rock was a figure of the Body of Christ, for it is written: "They drank of that rock that followed them, and that rock was Christ." Which certainly refers not to His Godhead, but to His Flesh, which watered the hearts of the thirsting people with the perpetual stream of His Blood. […]

"But I say unto you, that whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her, hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." "The humour," therefore, "is wiped off," when sin is not only severed from the deed, but also from the thought. It is hence that Jerubbaal saw the Angel when he was winnowing corn from the chaff, at whose bidding he forthwith dressed a kid and set it upon a rock, and poured over it the broth of the flesh, which the Angel touched with a rod, and thereupon fire coming out of the rock consumed it. For what else is it to beat corn with a rod, but to separate the grains of virtues from the chaff of vices, with an upright judgment? […]
6:19.s: Morals on the Book of Job 3.30.59

6:25.t: Then the man, instructed and fore-knowing what was to be, observes the heavenly mysteries, and therefore, according to the warning, slew the bullock destined by his father to idols, and himself offered to God another bullock seven years old. By doing which he most plainly showed that after the coming of the Lord all Gentile sacrifices should be done away, and that only the sacrifice of the Lord's passion should be offered for the redemption of the people. For that bullock was, in a type, Christ, in Whom, as Esaias said, dwelt the fulness of the seven gifts of the Spirit. This bullock Abraham also offered when he saw the day of the Lord and was glad. He it is Who was offered at one time in the type of a kid, at another in that of a sheep, at another in that of a bullock. […]

6:32.t: And where the Seventy put Jareb, we, following Symmachus, have translated "avenger"; for Aquila and Theodotion rendered "judge". That Jareb signifies avenger and judge, the name of Gideon shows: when the worshipers of Baal demanded him for punishment, because he had overthrown the grove and the altars of Baal, his father answered: Let Baal avenge himself, or let Baal judge him; and he was called, it says, Jerubbaal, that is: let Baal avenge himself.
Ierobaal [Jerubbaal]: let Baal judge, or having a judge, or superior, or having a quarrel.
6:32.s: On Hebrew Names, On the Book of Judges

6:33.t: "All Midian, therefore," it says, "and Amalek and the sons of the East gathered together and went up and came upon them and pitched their camp in the valley of Jezreel." These, who wish to assail the people of God, "pitch their camp in the valleys," in low and lowly places, "in the valley," it says, "of Jezreel." Now we find that Jezreel is interpreted as "the seed of God." Do you see where the adversaries "pitch their camp"? They did not dare to go there where the "fruits of the Spirit" are seen to have already been born, but where the seed of God still lies, where the fruit has not yet come up. […]

6:34.t: They, therefore, "pitch their camp in the valleys." "But the Spirit," it says, "of God strengthened Gideon, and he sounded the trumpet, upon the horn of the trumpet, and called Abiezer after him." The continuity of the exposition, indeed, required a different order, but because we are now speaking not so much to comment on the Scriptures as to console the people concerning those things which have been read, we treat here and there, as they occur, of individual points. "He called," it says, "Abiezer after him," who indeed was nowhere at all. Now "Abiezer" is interpreted as "the help of my father." Therefore Gideon seems to have called upon not some man, but the help of the highest Father. Meanwhile he also sends to summon reinforcements. […]

6:36.t: "And then," it says, "Gideon said to God: if you save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken, behold, here I am, and I will place a fleece of wool on the threshing-floor; and if indeed dew falls upon the fleece and there is dryness upon all the earth, I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken. And it was done so." Since there are so many and innumerable signs or prodigies which Gideon could have asked from God to confirm God's promise, why did it seem good to him, after the angelic voice and the heavenly promise, to ask of God this so novel a sign? For he says: "I will place a fleece of wool on the threshing-floor, and if there is dew upon the fleece only and dryness upon all the earth, I shall be confident that you will save Israel by my hand." […]

Some one perhaps will enquire whether he does not seem to have been wanting in faith, seeing that after being instructed by many signs he asked still more. But how can he seem to have asked as if doubting or wanting in faith, who was speaking in mysteries? He was not then doubtful, but careful that we should not doubt. For how could he be doubtful whose prayer was effectual? And how could he have begun the battle without fear, unless he had understood the message of God? for the dew on the fleece signified the faith among the Jews, because the words of God come down like the dew.

But what does this mean: "Until the day on which the Lord shall send rain on the earth"? except that he, too, "shall come down like rain upon a fleece, and like the drops that water the earth." In this passage the mystery of the old history is disclosed where Gideon, the warrior of the mystic conflict, receiving the pledge of future victory, recognized the spiritual sacrament in the vision of his mind, that that rain was the dew of the divine Word, which first came down on the fleece, when all the earth was parched with continual drought, and by a second true sign, moistened the floor of all the earth with a shower, while dryness was upon the fleece.

Again on this subject it is written: "For through the law comes the knowledge of sin. But now, apart from the law, the justice of God is made manifest, being witnessed by the law and the prophets." When he says "made manifest" he shows that it had existed but was like the dew for which Gideon asked; then it was not visible on the fleece, but now it is made manifest on the ground around. Therefore, since law without grace could only strengthen rather than kill sin—as it is written: "The sting of death is sin and the strength of sin is the law"—and as many flee to grace for refuge from the face of sin which had been so enthroned, to grace lying manifest, as it were, on the ground, so at that time few fled to it [grace] for refuge, invisible as it were, on the fleece. […]

But some, like the Jews in former times, both wish to be called Christians, and—still ignorant of God's righteousness—desire to establish their own, even in our own times of open grace, of the full revelation of grace that was previously hidden, that is, in the times of grace now manifested in the floor, which had before lay hidden in the fleece.… Gideon, one of the righteous men of old, asked for a sign from the Lord, and said, "I pray, Lord, that this fleece which I put on the floor would be wet with dew, and that the floor would be dry." And it was so. The fleece was wet with dew while the whole floor was dry. In the morning he wrung out the fleece in a basin—since grace is given to the humble—and you know what the Lord did to his disciples [with water] in a basin. […]

“And He shall come down like rain into a fleece, and like drops distilling upon the earth” (ver. 6). He hath called to our minds and admonished us, that what was done by Gedeon the Judge, in Christ hath its end. For he asked a sign of the Lord, that a fleece laid on the floor should alone be rained upon, and the floor should be dry; and again, the fleece alone should be dry, and the floor should be rained upon; and so it came to pass. Which thing signified, that, being as it were on a floor in the midst of the whole round world, the dry fleece was the former people Israel. The same Christ therefore Himself came down like rain upon a fleece, when yet the floor was dry: whence also He said, “I am not sent but to the sheep which were lost of the house of Israel.” […]

6:37.t: But that also, which Gideon says: "I will place the fleece" — not just anywhere, not in a field nor in a woodland, but "on the threshing-floor" — how does it seem to you? "On the threshing-floor," where the "harvest" is: "for the harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few." "I will place," he says, "the fleece" there, where the "harvest" is. What had moved the holy man Gideon, or what had seemed good to him, that he should do this? For he foresaw through the Spirit that Christ "gathers" his people "into the threshing-floor" and there cleanses him, "holding the winnowing-fan in his hand," and there separates the "chaff" from the wheat. […]

Nor was it without a reason that he put the fleece neither in a field nor in a meadow, but in a threshing-floor, where is the harvest of the wheat: "For the harvest is plenteous, but the labourers are few;" because that, through faith in the Lord, there was about to be a harvest fruitful in virtues.

Nor, again, was it without a reason that he dried the fleece of the Jews, and put the dew from it into a basin, so that it was filled with water, yet he did not himself wash his feet in that dew. The prerogative of so great a mystery was to be given to another. He was being waited for Who alone could wash away the filth of all. Gideon was not great enough to claim this mystery for himself, but "the Son of Man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister." Let us, then, recognize in Whom these mysteries are seen to be accomplished. Not in holy Gideon, for they were still at their commencement. Therefore the Gentiles were surpassed, for dryness was still upon the Gentiles, and therefore did Israel surpass them, for then did the dew remain on the fleece. […]

The nation of the Jews hath just so remained as a fleece dry upon the ground. For this, ye know, happened in a certain miracle, the ground was dry, the fleece only was wet, yet rain in the fleece appeared not. So also the mystery of the New Testament appeared not in the nation of the Jews. What there was the fleece, is here the veil. For in the fleece was veiled the mystery. But on the ground, in all the nations open lieth Christ’s Gospel; the rain is manifest, the Grace of Christ is bare, for it is not covered with a veil. But that the rain might come out of it, the fleece was pressed. For by pressure they from themselves excluded Christ, and the Lord now from His clouds raineth on the ground, the fleece hath remained dry.

In a certain nation were hidden the Law and the Prophets, “all the words of Thy mouth:” in the Jewish nation alone were “all the words of Thy mouth,” the nation which the Apostle praiseth, saying, “What advantage hath the Jew? Much every way; chiefly because that unto them were committed the oracles of God.” These were the words of God.…What meant Gideon’s fleece? It is like the nation of the Jews in the midst of the world, which had the grace of sacraments, not indeed openly manifested, but hidden in a cloud, or in a veil, like the dew in the fleece. The time came when the dew was to be manifested in the floor; it was manifested, no longer hidden. Christ alone is the sweetness of dew: Him alone thou recognisest not in Scripture, for whom Scripture was written.

A figure preceded in the fleece and dew of Gideon. The history is that Gideon asked of the Lord that the dew falling would be entirely on the fleece, and the threshing floor would remain dry; and he filled a basin with dew. Who brought it about that the Virgin conceived? Certainly the Holy Spirit, who is a love fervent, fruitful, undefiled, virile, incorrupt, and deifying. That he is an undefiled love is signified in the completed fleece, because the dew did not soil the fleece but cleansed it.

7:2.t: Vast was the multitude that had been gathered against Israel, so great that for its number it was compared to "locusts". "And their camels", it says, "were like the sand which is beyond number upon the shore of the sea". Let us see, then, how so countless a multitude of enemies could be overcome: there went out, it says, thirty-two thousand armed men from the sons of Israel with Gideon to fight against all that multitude. And God gave answer to Gideon, saying: "The multitude that is with you is great". And what if "the multitude is great"? Does not a more numerous army in wars afford safer defenses? By no means, He says, for divine battles are not carried out as human ones are. […]

Against the Midianites also, who, as the Book of Judges relates, had filled all the land like locusts, Gideon was ordered to fight with a few men, not because he had not more in his army, but he was forbidden to lead many men to battle for fear that a multitude might claim some share in the victory as their own. When Gideon had gathered together thirty thousand armed men, the Lord spoke thus to him: "The people that are with thee are too many for me to give Midian into their hands." What followed? He left Gideon, to fight against countless thousands of barbarians, only three hundred men. Indeed, he commanded the force of soldiers to be reduced to such a scanty number in order that their lack of men might prevent any claim of credit for a victory divinely won. […]
7:2.s: On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapters 8-9

7:3.t: Therefore speak in the ears of the people, saying: Whoever is timid and fearful of heart, let him return. And there returned from Mount Gilead, out of the people, twenty-two thousand men, and there remained ten thousand. Let us see, then, first, what it means that He says: "timid and fearful of heart"; for two things are named by which human frailty is convicted, that is, the "timid" and the "fearful" of heart. He may seem "timid" who at the first sight trembles at the encounter, yet is not terrified with his whole heart, but can be restored and heartened again. […]

O ye who have been called to the conflict, hear the sound of the trumpet and be of good cheer. And also I speak to you, bearers of the trumpets, priests, doctors and wise men, assemble and say to all the people: "He who fears let him turn away from the conflict, lest he break the heart of his brethren, even as his heart (is broken). And he who has planted a vineyard let him return to his husbandry, lest being anxious about it he fail in the battle. And he who has married a wife and wishes to take her, let him return and rejoice with his wife. And he who has built a house let him return to it, lest perhaps he be mindful of his house and does not fight perfectly". […]

7:4.t: But after these "twenty-two thousand departed", the divine discourse adds still further and "says to Gideon": "Still", it says, "the people are many; bring them down to the water, and there I will test them for you". As I see it, those who were first rejected had not even gone down "into the water", but were still marking themselves out as catechumens, and were so deterred by the vice of dread that they did not even go down to the saving washing: those, then, were rejected in this way. But these second ones come "to the water", that they may be tested there. And how they are tested, let us see:

7:5.t: "And the Lord said", it says, "to Gideon: everyone who shall lap the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set him apart; and everyone who shall bend his knees to drink, you shall set him aside. And the number", it says, "of those who lapped the water in their hand or with the tongue was three hundred men, but all the rest bent their knees to drink the water. And the Lord said to Gideon: by these three hundred men who lapped I will save you and deliver Midian into your hand". […]

Dogs should not always be taken in an evil sense; otherwise the prophet would not blame "dogs not able to bark and loving to dream." Doubtless they would be praiseworthy dogs if they both knew how to bark and loved to watch. And certainly those three hundred men—a most sacred number according to the letter of the cross10—would not have been chosen to win the victory because they lapped water as dogs do, unless some great mystery were signified. Good dogs watch and bark to protect their house and their master, their flock and their shepherd. Finally, even here in the praises offered by the church, when a selection is made from this prophecy, it is the tongue of dogs that is mentioned, not their teeth.

Not only “of dogs” he hath said, but “of Thy dogs:” nor are their teeth praised, but their tongue is: for it was not indeed to no purpose, not without a great mystery, that Gedeon was bidden to lead those alone, who should lap the water of the river like dogs; and of such sort not more than three hundred among so great a multitude were found. In which number is the sign of the Cross because of the letter T, which in the Greek numeral characters signifieth three hundred.

And they are brought to the river, to drink the waters; and whoever drank the waters with bended knees, were removed from the struggle of war. For by the waters is designated the doctrine of wisdom, but by the unbended knee righteous conduct. They therefore who are reported to have bent their knees, while drinking the water, retired from the strife of battles, having been forbidden; because Christ proceeds to battle against the enemies of the faith, with those who when they drink the streams of doctrine, distort not the uprightness of their actions. For all are said at that time to have drunk the water, but not all to have stood with unbended knee. […]
7:5.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 30.74

7:6.t: This was marked in the case of Gedeon where those who were tested by the water, that is, those who lapped it like dogs, fought the battle and won, while those who bent their knee to drink were turned away. And those who had won the test were given trumpets and pitchers and lanterns, and they obtained the victory by means of blaring horns and clanging vessels. These are the preachers of the Church who in their preaching make a blaring of horns. The vessels are the bodies, the lanterns are the miracles. Indeed, every time they died for the sake of truth, they repelled and overcame the enemy by means of miracles. But those who drink by lapping with their tongues like dogs, who draw only a little water with their tongues, are those who take little from philosophy; […]

7:7.t: Just as the six hundred years of life which Noah completed prior to entering the ark designate the perfection of faith and confession of those who approach the church's sacraments of heavenly grace and perpetual reward, so also does the three hundred and fifty years that he lived after the great flood typify the perfection of those who, having received the sacraments of life, zealously and faithfully serve the Lord until death. For we say that three hundred, because it is denoted in Greek by the letter tau, which is written in the shape of a cross, most aptly signifies those who resolve not to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. […]

7:15.t: I think it will not be amiss if we consider at greater length this war of the Madianites, which was intentionally introduced by the Prophet in comparison with the coming of the Lord. For in the book of Judges Gedeon is described as having fought against the Madianites. When he was bringing forth the multitude of the army to war, he was ordered by a Divine admonition, to remove from the conflict of battle all whom on coming to the water he beheld drinking the water with bended knees. And the result was, that only three hundred men remained, who had drunk the water in their hands, standing. With these he proceeds to the battle, and he equipped them not with arms, but with trumpets, lamps, and pitchers. […]
7:15.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 30, Section 73

7:16.t: Yet how do these fight? "Pitchers", it says, they carry, "and lamps and horn trumpets in their hands", and thus, it says, they come against those countless multitudes of the enemy, among whom were "camels like the sand of the sea". And when they had come to the battle, "with the horn trumpets", it says, "they sounded". And they let go the "pitchers" from their hands, and "they were shattered". But then, snatching up the lamps, they rush upon the adversaries, and at the same time crash out with the trumpets. See how the chosen soldiers of God fight with lamps. For thus had Christ armed them, saying: "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning", and again: "So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven". […]

For the same reason was it that when Gideon was about to overcome the Midianites, he commanded three hundred men to take pitchers, and to hold lighted torches inside the pitchers, and trumpets in their right hands. Our predecessors have preserved the explanation received from the apostles, that the pitchers are our bodies, fashioned of clay, which do not know fear if they burn with the fervor of the grace of the Spirit, and bear witness to the passion of the Lord Jesus with a loud confession of the voice. Who, then, can doubt the divinity of the Holy Spirit, since where the grace of the Spirit is, there the manifestation of the divinity appears. By this evidence we infer not a diversity but the unity of the divine power. […]

7:20.t: They go forth therefore to battle with trumpets, with lamps, and with pitchers. This, as we have said, was an unusual order of battle. They sounded with the trumpets, and the pitchers were held in their left hands. But lamps were placed within the pitchers; but, when the pitchers were broken, the lamps appeared, and by their flashing light the affrighted enemies are put to flight. By the trumpets is designated therefore the loud voice of preachers, by the lamps the brightness of their miracles, by the pitchers the frailness of their bodies. For our Leader led forth with Him, to the contest of preaching, such as by making light of their bodily safety, would overthrow their enemies by dying, and would overcome their swords, not by arms, not by words, but by patience. […]
7:20.s: Morals on the Book of Job 30.25

9:8.t: And no one has been so illiterate as to think that similar fables of Aesop, related for the same purpose, ought to be called lies. But also in the sacred writings such passages are found, as in the book of Judges the trees look for a king to rule over them and speak to the olive and the fig and the vine and the bramble. Surely, all this is invented in order that we may reach the matter intended by means of a narrative [that is] fictitious, to be sure, but bearing a true and not a false signification.

11:30.t: Also Jephthah was persecuted, as Jesus was persecuted. Jephthah, his brethren drove out from the house of his father; and Jesus, His brethren drove out and lifted up and crucified. Jephthah though persecuted arose as leader to his people; Jesus though persecuted arose and became King of the Nations. Jephthah vowed a vow and offered up his firstborn daughter as a sacrifice; and Jesus was lifted up as a sacrifice to his Father for all the Gentiles.

SINCE ABRAHAM WAS FORBIDDEN TO SACRIFICE HIS SON, WHY WAS JEPHTHAH NOT FORBIDDEN TO CARRY OUT THE SACRIFICE OF HIS DAUGHTER? (Gen. 22:11–12; Judg. 11)? — There is a great difference between Abraham’s case and Jephthah’s case. First, Abraham was legitimately born, whereas Jephthah was illegitimate, for he was the son of a prostitute. Next, Abraham was of excellent conduct, but Jephthah was a leader of bandits. Abraham was a righteous man, proven in temptation; in Jephthah, however, there is no testimony of righteousness. Abraham, therefore, was commanded to offer his son to God so that it might be shown to people how greatly Abraham trusted God, since at His command he did not hesitate even to kill his own son. […]
11:30.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 43: ON JEPHTHAH'S VOW AND ABRAHAM'S SACRIFICE

11:30.t: And whereas he [Jovinianus] prefers the fidelity of the father Jephthah to the tears of the virgin daughter, that corroborates our point. For we are not commending virgins of the world so much as those who are virgins for Christ's sake. Most Hebrews blame the father for the rash vow he made, "If you will indeed deliver the children of Ammon into my hand, then it shall be that whatsoever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me, when I return in peace from the children of Ammon, it shall be for the Lord's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering." Supposing (the Hebrews say) a dog or an ass had met him, what would he have done? Their meaning is that God so ordered events that he who had improvidently made a vow should learn his error by the death of his daughter.

11:35.t: The remaining sacrifices, of which those relating to the law are a symbol, are akin to this sacrifice. But in addition, the other sacrifices akin to this sacrifice seem to me to be the shedding of the blood of the noble martyrs. It was not in vain that the disciple John saw them standing beside the heavenly altar. "But who is wise, that he shall understand these things? Or intelligent, and he shall know them?"3Now comprehend, even if to a limited extent, the more spiritual sense of such sacrifices which cleanse those for whom they are offered; one must understand the sense of the sacrifice of the daughter of Jephthah who was offered as a burnt offering because of the vow of him who conquered the children of Ammon. […]
11:35.s: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6.276-78

11:39.t: It is also sometimes contrary to duty to fulfill a promise or to keep an oath. As was the case with Herod, who swore that whatever was asked he would give to the daughter of Herodias, and so allowed the death of John, that he might not break his word. And what shall I say of Jephthah, who offered up his daughter in sacrifice, she having been the first to meet him as he returned home victorious; whereby he fulfilled the vow which he had made that he would offer to God whatever should meet him first. It would have been better to make no promise at all than to fulfill it in the death of his daughter.
11:39.s: On the Duties of the Clergy 1.50.255

11:39.t: Never shall I be led to believe that the leader Jephthah made his vow otherwise than without thought, when he promised to offer to God whatever should meet him at the threshold of his house on his return. For he repented of his vow, as afterwards his daughter came to meet him. He tore his clothes and said, "Alas, my daughter, you have entangled me, you have become a source of trouble for me."
